html:
The Dust Bowl was a time of terrible dust storms on the southern Great Plains of the United States in the 1930s. Drought killed the crops, and the wind lifted the bare soil into black clouds.

The cause was partly human. In the decades before, farmers had ploughed up millions of acres of prairie grass to grow wheat, helped by tractors and high grain prices. The grass roots had held the soil in place. When severe drought came in the early 1930s, nothing was left to hold it.

The worst storm, on "Black Sunday" in April 1935, turned day to night across Oklahoma and Texas. Hundreds of thousands of people left the plains, many heading for California, where they were called "Okies". John Steinbeck told their story in The Grapes of Wrath.

It struck at the same time as the Great Depression. As part of the New Deal, Franklin D. Roosevelt's government set up the Soil Conservation Service, paid farmers to change how they ploughed, and planted belts of trees to break the wind. Later, center pivot irrigation brought the dry plains back into crops.
sum: The Dust Bowl was a time of terrible dust storms on the southern Great Plains of the United States in the 1930s. Drought killed the crops, and the wind lifted the bare soil into black clouds.
